chapter: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
title: First dance job in Brewton and the man with the pistol
summary: He talks his religious mother into letting him play a dance in Brewton, sees trap drums for the first time, and a gunman scares the one-eyed clarinetist.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: No. Ma Rainey, that's different, but I knew Ma Rainey, played for her. Sure. Knew Ma Rainey. And the minstrel -- you asked me the first job, they gave a dance in Brewton, Alabama, that was about 20 miles from Evergreen. And they were short of a man. They needed somebody to be the trumpet player, and so they got ahold of me and asked me to come down and join them. And I'd never played a dance before in my life.
And, well, the argument was talk your mom into it.

She said, well, I don't know, and maybe but -- I said, but Mother, that's a chance. She said, but in a dance hall, and she couldn't see it. Nothing about in the dance hall, but when you mention the dance hall, it was out, you know. I mean a preacher's daughter --
And was she a religious woman herself?

Oh! Very much so, yeah. And finally I talked her into letting me go, and I went down to play this dance hall, and in this dance hall with these lights and, you know, the guys in there tuning up their horns and a piano. I never played with a piano before. Had a banjo, clarinet, and the first time I'd ever seen a man play trap drums. That's what they called them then. And it was usually -- in a minstrel show it was one guy playing the snare and played it, you know, on the shoulder, and the guy with the bass drums and the cymbals, you know.

But this was all in one, and I was amazed, and he was doggone good too. And we started playing, and everything, to my mind, everything was going fine, and a big man, huge guy walked in the door and pulled out one of those big Texas pistols, I call it.
Yes. He says, don't a man make a move until I make this shot! And, well -- pss-s-s-s -- people

So the clarinet player -- I never forget this -- he jumped behind me and he said, 'now don't move. Don't move. Stand still now. Don't get excited. Don't move. Stand right there. This is how I lost my eye.' He was one eyed.
Jesus, this is how I lost my eye. Somebody stuck him struck me in the eye in the dark. And I said, you're hiding behind me?
Man, don't move. Stand right here and protect me, he's saying to himself. And he was an older man. And I was just -- a little boy. Well, nothing happened, but --
